items.english: It is hot. Sweat wells prickling up on his forehead, and when it seems to have beaded it comes trickling lukewarm toward his eyes. As ill luck will have it he is bound with thin cord, so of course he cannot put out a hand to wipe it away. He tries moving his neck to turn the sweat from its path, but at that instant he feels a violent dizziness about to come on, so to his regret he gives up that plan too. Meanwhile the sweat unreservedly wets his eyelids, and circling from the side of his nose round his mouth, runs down under his chin. The nastiness is beyond measure.
notes: Kept the opening present tense and the long cumulative sweat sentences long; the short close is kept short and flat.

items.english: Until then he had kept his eyes open, gazing hard at the sky scorched white and the hemp-field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to pour without restraint he had to give even that up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets into the eyes. So, wearing the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, meekly shutting his eyes while he lies still beneath the beating sun, he begins by degrees to feel a certain pain in the skin of the upper parts of him, face or body alike. Over the whole surface of the skin a force is at work urging it to move in every direction at once, while the skin itself has not the least elasticity to answer it with; a pain that might best be described as a smarting everywhere. This is not the misery of mere sweating. Liu began to feel a little bitter at having taken the barbarian monk's cure.
notes: 汗所 rendered as 'mere sweating' — literal sense uncertain, left flat rather than medicalized.
Narrator's 'to Betsu suru' hedge kept as 'might best be described as'.

items.english: Yet this, as he came to think afterward, was still of the less painful order. — Before long his throat grew parched. Liu too knows the tale of how Cao Mengde, or someone, doctored his soldiers' thirst by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But in this present case, however he pictures the sweet-sour plum in his mind, his throat is thirsty just the same as before. He moves his chin, he bites his tongue, but the inside of his mouth still holds its heat. Even that might have been a little easier to bear, had it not been for the unglazed jar at his pillow. For from the mouth of the jar the rich fumes of wine assail his nose without pause. And, perhaps only in fancy, that reek seems to grow stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opens his eyes. Straining them upward, he takes in the mouth of the jar and perhaps half of its generously swollen belly. That is all he takes in with his eyes, but at the same time there rises in his imagination the golden-yellow wine lying brimful and still in the jar's dim interior. Before he knows it he licks his cracked lips round with his dry tongue, but there is no sign of saliva welling. Even his sweat by now is dried by the sun and no longer flows as before.
notes: Cao Mengde allusion glossed in line only, as 'telling them there was a plum grove ahead', without further history.
上眼 rendered as straining the eyes upward from a bound, supine position.

items.english: Then violent dizziness comes, two or three times in succession. The headache has been unbroken since a while back. In his heart Liu curses the barbarian monk ever more bitterly. And then he thinks too why a man such as himself should have ridden on such a fellow's cajolery into this idiotic suffering. Meanwhile his throat grows ever thirstier. His chest turns strangely queasy. He can no longer lie still for endurance. So at last, resolving himself, Liu opens his gasping mouth, meaning to beg the monk at his pillow to stop the cure. —

But at that very instant. Liu begins to feel an unnameable lump creeping little by little up from his breast toward his throat. At one moment it seems to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge itself along like a gecko. In any case some soft thing, soft as it is, comes squirming up the gullet. And at last, when it seems to have forced its way beneath his Adam's apple, all at once it slips like a loach or something out of the dark and flies outwards with force.
notes: Kept the odd simile sequence earthworm-gecko-loach in order, without unifying or prettifying.

items.english: At that moment, from the quarter of that same unglazed jar, comes a small plop, as of something dropping into wine.
At this the monk abruptly lifts the haunches he had settled and begins to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm is out now, he says, he may rest easy.

"Is it out?" Liu says this as if groaning, and raising his reeling head, out of curiosity forgets even his thirst and crawls naked to the side of the jar. Seeing it, Sun Sensei too, shading the sun with his white-feather fan, hurries toward the two. When all three peer together into the jar, there is a small thing like a salamander, its flesh the colour of red clay, swimming in the wine. It must be about three sun in length. It has a mouth, it has eyes. Somehow it seems to drink as it swims. Seeing this, Liu suddenly feels sick. ...
notes: 'Three sun' kept as period measure, about nine centimetres, left to context.
Worm kept as 'thing like a salamander' with mouth and eyes; not ennobled to spirit or demon.

data.say: Drafted the ordeal in long cumulative sentences with present-tense bodily sensation preserved.
